newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow confirms leak but says not fuel, crew fine.
newsitem.headline: Moscow confirms leak but says not fuel, crew fine.

text.p: A senior official at Mission Control said on Saturday there had been a mystery leak into space from a holed module on Russia's crippled Mir orbital station five days ago but experts were sure it was not fuel.
"Only one thing is clear -- it was not fuel," the senior communications specialist told Reuters on condition he not be identified. "Apart from that no one has an answer yet to this mystery."

Veteran astronaut Frank Culbertson, who runs the U.S. NASA space agency's missions to Mir, said earlier there had been an as yet unexplained incident and that it raised new questions about carrying out repairs on the damaged vessel.
"We are very concerned about what was in that module, what might have ruptured, and what the impact might be on the suited crew members," he told a news conference in the United States.
The Russian specialist said: "Five days ago, in one of our communications with the crew, we were told they had seen flakes and bubbles from an unknown source leaking from the Spektr module."
The leak had been into space rather than inside, and there had been no repeat since that single incident. He did not say why there had been a delay in reporting the leak.

The crew ran into trouble on June 25 when a Progress cargo craft hit the station during a manual docking and punctured the Spektr science module -- the worst accident since Mir was first blasted into its orbit around the Earth more than 11 years ago.

News of the latest incident broke just hours after a new Progress tug was launched to take a repair kit and other supplies to the three-man crew -- commander Vasily Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin of Russia and British-born U.S. astronaut Michael Foale.
The specialist, speaking from Mission Control at Korolyov near Moscow, said experts were analysing data from the crew.
"We do not have any information on the situation inside the Spektr module," he said. "Measurements show there have been no other leaks in the other modules and sections of the station."
He said the three men were feeling fine and had spent the day making checks ready for the arrival of the cargo craft.
Sunday would be a rest day.

The new craft is scheduled to dock with Mir on Monday. Once the crew have trained properly, they face a tricky repair job to try to restore full power to the sprawling station, which has gradually grown through the addition of various modules.
The supplies aboard the unmanned Progress M-35 include oxygen, food and water as well as the tools needed to save the station after it lost up to half its electric power.

Flight director Vladimir Solovyov said the craft would dock automatically. He told reporters: "We will follow Progress carefully today and prepare it for docking, scheduled for Monday July 7 at 0959 Moscow time (0559 GMT)."
Experts say the overall lack of power on Mir will make the docking operation for Progress problematic. One of four solar panels on the Spektr module was damaged in the collision.
Even after Monday's docking, the crew face a long and uncomfortable wait of nearly two weeks before attempting the risky electrical repairs during a spacewalk.
Solovyov told Russia's Vremya television news programme the crew had been despondent after the collision.
"But they pulled themselves together, stopped reproaching themselves," he said. "Now they work very energetically and effectively."
